title: Devarim: how can I alone? (Deuteronomy 1:12)
hook: Moses' "how" is chanted to the tune of Lamentations before Tisha B'Av

segments.voice: Yesterday, Devarim and the judges' charge: a penny case as precious as a fortune. Your line was small and great alike. Today, one word changes the music in the synagogue.

It's the Sabbath just before Tisha B'Av, the fast that mourns the destruction of the Temples in Jerusalem. The reader at the Torah is chanting Devarim in the usual melody, the one the congregation has heard all year. Then, on one verse, the tune turns. It drops into a slow, sad melody that everyone in the room recognizes. It's the melody of the book of Lamentations, which they'll hear on the floor in the dim light a few days later. All on account of a single word.
screen: `THE SABBATH BEFORE TISHA B'AV.` → `THE TUNE TURNS ON ONE VERSE.` → `THE MELODY OF LAMENTATIONS.`

segments.voice: The verse is Moses, remembering how worn out he was in the wilderness. In the old Jewish translation: "How can I myself alone bear your cumbrance, and your burden, and your strife?" The first word in Hebrew is eicha. How. Not a calm how, like how do I fix this. A cry. And it's the same word that opens the book of Lamentations: "How doth the city sit solitary, that was full of people!" That book is even called Eicha in Hebrew. The midrash on Lamentations noticed that three prophets used this word: Moses here, Isaiah looking at a faithful city gone wrong, and Jeremiah over the ruins of Jerusalem. Moses saw the people at ease, the midrash says, Isaiah saw them restless, and Jeremiah saw them broken. So the reader borrows Lamentations' melody for Moses' verse, and the whole room hears where the road can lead. But look at what Moses does with his eicha. He doesn't just sigh. He divides the load. He tells the people to bring wise, understanding men from each tribe, and he makes them heads over thousands and hundreds and fifties and tens. The path met this weariness twice already this year, with Jethro's advice and with the seventy elders. Deuteronomy tells it from Moses' own side, years later, and lets one word carry the feeling. In this story, saying how can I alone isn't a failure. It's the sentence that comes right before help.
screen: `EICHA: HOW, AS A CRY.` · `THE FIRST WORD OF LAMENTATIONS.` · `MOSES, ISAIAH, JEREMIAH.` · `HE DIVIDES THE LOAD.` · then, large: `HOW CAN I ALONE?`

segments.voice: Let your mind go to whatever has been too heavy lately: a sick parent, a project, a child who's struggling. Don't solve it; just say quietly, the way Moses did, how can I alone, and let it be a sigh, not a plan. Then let one name come to mind, someone you could say it to.
Eicha. How, as a cry. Moses' word in Deuteronomy, and the first word and Hebrew name of the book of Lamentations.
Your line: how can I alone. Even Moses needed others to share the load. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: On the Sabbath before Tisha B'Av, many congregations chant Deuteronomy 1:12, which begins with eicha, in the mournful melody used for the book of Lamentations on Tisha B'Av itself.

original.note: Hebrew: how. a cry, not a question. it opens Deuteronomy 1:12 and the book of Lamentations.

chat.says: Why does the Torah reader switch to a sad tune on one verse before Tisha B'Av?
options: It opens with eicha, how, the same word that begins Lamentations.
Moses was mourning the Temple, which had fallen in his own day.
That verse is a curse, and every curse gets the sad tune.
chat.meaning: Deuteronomy 1:12 begins with eicha, the word that opens Lamentations, so the reader borrows Lamentations' melody for it.

notes: Audit (10% sample): the close of the teach, the practice and the carry repeated day 444 (share one burden, hand off a piece) and day 343 (Jethro). The teach now names those days as callbacks, and the practice and carry move to saying the eicha honestly and naming the load to one person.
Deuteronomy 1:12 and Lamentations 1:1 quoted from JPS 1917 from memory; verify.
Lamentations Rabbah 1:1 on three prophets who said eicha (Moses, Isaiah, Jeremiah), with Moses seeing Israel in tranquility, Isaiah in restlessness, Jeremiah in disgrace; paraphrased, confirm.
Custom of chanting Deuteronomy 1:12 in the Lamentations melody on Shabbat Chazon is widespread (Ashkenazi and many others); Keeper may want to note variation in custom.
Tisha B'Av described as mourning the destruction of the Temples; it also commemorates other calamities.
